source_read: PMC HTML, PMC11582610 (Sci Rep 2024;14:28817), read in full in my own browser tab: get_page_text returned the whole article (81,706 characters, under the 120,000 limit), saved to my scratch folder and read from there: abstract, introduction, methods (Studies 1 and 2), results with Tables 1-4, discussion, data availability, declarations and references. Fig. 1 (stacked bars of all 26 ReCiPE items) is an image and was not needed: the percentages the claim uses are printed in the Results text. Supplementary Material S.I-S.VII (a .docx) was not read.

claims.overstatement: The Wood figures are reported as recalled judgments of helpfulness, which is what they are. Three wording points. (1) 'Acceptance-type responses' follows the authors' factor label, but the score is a count of 11 items judged helpful, which besides letting go and observing includes telling the experience to stop, directing anger at it, questioning it, journaling, focusing on breathing, closing the eyes, asking forgiveness and calling on spirits or a deity (Table 2 loadings; Reliability paragraph). (2) 'On which two independent surveys agree' is loose: the surveys used different lists; they agree only that calming or accepting responses were the ones most often reported as helpful, and Wood prints percentages for just seven of its 26 items. (3) Inclusion was a classic psychedelic 'or analogue', with combined use of MDMA or ketamine allowed. The authors themselves overstate: the Discussion opens by saying the study examined the effectiveness of strategies and says the correlations confirm that breakthrough involves more helpful strategies; the claim does not repeat this.
claims.note: Numbers checked against the Results text: 84.5%, 77.3%, 73.9%; 9.4%, 9.7%, 10.6%, 12.1% (of 529, tried and judged somewhat or substantially helpful). r = 0.50 between the Acceptance and Reappraisal count and the EBI average (Table 3, p < .001). Study 1: 16 participants, inclusion required self-reported significant personal transformation together with distress during ceremonies. The 'evasive reassurance' quote is P11 (sub-theme 4.3), who in the next quote found the lead guide's reassurance very reassuring.

anchors.extracted: Adults 18 or over, proficient in English, with prior psychedelic experience; both studies were online Qualtrics surveys; neither was pre-registered.

anchors.locator: Methods › Study 2: online survey › Participants and recruitment
anchors.extracted: Recruited through an online survey advertised via targeted social media, research groups and user forums; inclusion: at least one experience with a classic psychedelic or analogue (psilocybin, ayahuasca, LSD, DMT, mescaline); MDMA-, ketamine- or other non-classic-only experiences excluded, combined use allowed.

anchors.locator: Methods › Study 2: online survey › Measures › Responses to challenging psychedelic experiences
anchors.extracted: ReCiPE: 26 items derived from the Study 1 themes and the literature; each rated not tried / tried, not helpful / somewhat helpful / substantially helpful; for analysis scored 1 only if tried and at least somewhat helpful, so scores are counts of strategies judged helpful, not degrees of helpfulness.

anchors.locator: Results › Study 2: online survey › Descriptive statistics, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: 869 completed the survey; 555 reported a challenge (printed 64.24%; 555/869 = 63.9%); 529 (95.31%) gave data for analysis: 243 men (45.94%), 256 women (48.39%), 30 non-binary or other (5.67%); mean age 37.71 (SD 10.88).

anchors.locator: Results › Study 2: online survey › Descriptive statistics, 2nd paragraph (Fig. 1)
anchors.extracted: Tried and judged somewhat or substantially helpful, of 529: letting go, accepting or surrendering 84.5%; observing the mind and not fighting it 77.3%; closing eyes, lying or sitting down 73.9%. Least often: directing anger or aggression at the challenge 9.4%; trying to fall asleep 9.7%; telling it to stop or go away 10.6%; taking another drug or alcohol 12.1%.

anchors.locator: Results › Study 2: online survey › Descriptive statistics, 3rd paragraph
anchors.extracted: On average 11.25 (SD 4.78) strategies judged helpful per person (mode 10).

anchors.locator: Table 2 and Results › Study 2 › Reliability, 2nd paragraph
anchors.extracted: Factor 1 (Acceptance and Reappraisal) counts 11 items: letting go, observing, questioning the challenge, telling it to stop (loading below 0.4, kept), anger or aggression towards it (0.43), interpreting sensations as meaningful, journaling, breathing, closing eyes (cross-loading), asking forgiveness, calling on spirits or a deity. Factor 2 has 10 items, Factor 3 five.
Correlations with the EBI average: Acceptance and Reappraisal 0.50 (p < .001); Sensory Regulation 0.18 (p < .001); Social Support 0.27 (p < .001); CEQ fear -0.14, grief 0.41, death 0.20.

anchors.locator: Results › Study 2 › Multiple regression, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Table 4
anchors.extracted: EBI on fear, grief, physical distress, death and the three ReCiPE counts: F(7, 519) = 50.93, adjusted R2 0.40; Acceptance and Reappraisal beta 0.33 (p < .001), Social Support 0.07 (p = .041), Sensory Regulation 0.02 (p = .527); predictors chosen because they correlated with the outcome.

anchors.locator: Methods › Study 1: qualitative analysis › Participants and recruitment
anchors.extracted: Psilocybin retreat attendees at four centres in the Netherlands and Mexico, recruited by email among those who had agreed to be contacted; inclusion required self-reported significant personal transformation together with distress or difficulty during ceremonies.

16 participants (8 Netherlands, 8 Mexico); retreats of 3-7 days with up to 3 ceremonies; median 6 months since; mean age 45; 9 women, 7 men; 13 without religious affiliation; 15 with graduate or postgraduate education.

Written accounts of intentional breathing, opening the eyes and moving, engaging with the surroundings, asking for help, facilitators' touch and reminders to breathe, and listening. Under reassurance, one participant found a guide's 'you are where you need to be' answer to a factual question unhelpful and, in the next quote, the lead guide's reassurance very helpful.
Both samples self-selected, mostly experienced users from Western cultures; reports retrospective, in some cases several years after the experience; Study 1 selected for personal transformation.

The authors describe the study as examining the 'effectiveness' of strategies and say the correlations confirm that breakthrough involves more helpful strategies, wording that goes beyond recalled, cross-sectional data.

claims.overstatement: None. 'The experience they described' is right: the question was about the respondent's reported experience, and the paper does not say how that experience was chosen. 'Which shows how much the figure depends on who is asked and how' is the editors' reading, fair given the self-selected forum sample and the different question.
claims.note: 555/869 = 63.9%, as the claim's magnitude says. The paper prints 64.24%, which is 555/864: an arithmetic error in the source, not in the claim.

anchors.locator: Results › Study 2: online survey › Descriptive statistics, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Of 869 who completed the survey, 555 reported some challenge during their psychedelic experience (printed 64.24%; 63.9% by recomputation); 529 of the 555 analysed.

anchors.locator: Methods › Study 2: online survey › Measures › Challenging psychedelic experiences
anchors.extracted: Respondents were first asked whether they had any period of distress, difficulty or discomfort during their reported psychedelic experience; only those who said yes completed the CEQ.

anchors.locator: Methods › Study 2: online survey › Participants and recruitment; Measures › Demographic and contextual factors
anchors.extracted: Self-selected through social media, research groups and user forums; the substance and the time since the experience were recorded (reported only in the supplement), but how the reported experience was chosen is not stated.

key_findings.correction: Confirmed. Worth adding: item 4 (telling the experience to stop) was kept in Factor 1, Acceptance and Reappraisal, and item 5 (anger or aggression, loading 0.43) belongs to it as well (bold markup in Table 2; Reliability, 1st paragraph).
Values confirmed. Table 3 does not print its n; 529 is an assumption (the regression used 527).

reporting_issues.note: Found independently: t times SE gives B of -4.46 (fear), 7.04 (grief), 2.63 (death), 4.14 (acceptance), 1.23 (social support); the intercept row 29.33/3.30 = 8.89 is B.
Rescaled interval for acceptance recomputed: B 4.14 (3.16 to 5.12) times 0.33/4.14 gives 0.25 to 0.41. The fear interval (-0.30 to -0.14 around -0.24) is lopsided too.

risk_of_bias.note: ROBINS-E very high for Study 2: no covariates; exposure (strategies judged helpful) and outcome (EBI) rated retrospectively by the same person; predictors chosen by significance. Describing Study 1 without a rating is reasonable.

interpretation_gap.note: 'Substantial' fits: 'effectiveness', 'confirming', mediation language without mediation analysis, safety claims with no safety outcome, and standardized betas read as raw slopes. The limitations are frank.

missed: The 'Acceptance and Reappraisal' count (Factor 1, 11 items) includes two responses that are the opposite of acceptance: assertively telling the experience to stop or go away (item 4, loading 0.17, kept) and directing anger or aggression at it (item 5, 0.43). It also includes questioning the challenge, journaling, breathing, closing the eyes, asking forgiveness and calling on spirits or a deity (Table 2, bold markup; Results › Study 2 › Reliability, 1st paragraph). So r = 0.50 with breakthrough is for this mixed count, not for acceptance alone, which matters for the paper's conclusion and for any claim that speaks of 'acceptance-type responses'.

Two different percentages for the same strategies should not be confused: the Descriptive statistics percentages (84.5% and so on) are of all 529 and fold together 'tried' and 'judged helpful'; how many tried each strategy but found it unhelpful is only in Fig. 1 and supplement S.VII.
